title: Bhusuku Becomes a Bengali
summary: A vajra boat is rowed across a lotus canal, and the poet loses everything. Nondual Baṅgāla plunders his affliction, a Caṇḍāla takes his wife, his gold, his silver and his storehouse of four crores are gone, and living and dying are no different to him; the refrain says that today Bhusuku has become a Bengali. Munidatta says the poet teaches under the guise of a Bengali woman (cp.49.m1), and reads Baṅgāla as nondual imperishable bliss (cp.49.m2), the Caṇḍāla as clear light (cp.49.m3), gold and silver as grasping at emptiness and at being (cp.49.m5), and the storehouse as examination by the four alternatives (cp.49.m6).

flags.note: The Tibetan heading adds tA la gcig pa, probably a tāla (rhythmic cycle), 'one beat'. The Bengali does not have it, so it is left out of the English and recorded in a witness note. The poet's name comes from the attribution bhusukupādānām, 'of Bhusukupāda', which was emended out of 1a. The Tibetan heading names him too (b+hu su ku'i zhabs).

lines.translit: bāja ṇāba pāṛī pam̐uā khālem̐ bāhiu
lines.gloss: vajra · boat · crossing · lotus (or Padmā) · canal-on · rowed

flags.note: I read bāja as vajra, giving 'vajra boat'. The Tibetan line has rgyal po'i gru, 'the king's boat', as though it read রাজ rāja: র differs from ব only by the dot beneath. Munidatta's comment on this couplet (cp.49.m2) has no lemma, so it does not cite the word. I chose vajra as the plain reading of the Bengali; 'the king's boat' is the alternative.

pam̐uā can be the lotus (padma) or the river Padmā. I chose 'lotus' because both old witnesses read the flower: Munidatta's paraphrase has the lotus of wisdom (prajñāravinda, cp.49.m2), and the Tibetan line has pad+ma'i tshal, 'lotus grove'. 'Rowed across the Padmā canal' would suit the geography of Baṅgāla in 1b, but it would need a new place entry.

I took pāṛī as the noun 'crossing' (Bengali pāṛi, a crossing of a river) and rendered it 'across'. It could also be an absolutive, 'having crossed'. bāhiu is taken as a passive participle, 'was rowed', in line with Munidatta's vāhita (cp.49.m2). The song does not name the rower.

lines.gloss: nondual (advaya; or pitiless, adaya)-Baṅgāla-by · affliction · plundered

flags.note: adaa can stand for advaya, 'nondual', or for adaya, 'pitiless'; either would become adaa in Old Bengali. I chose 'nondual'. Munidatta reads advayavaṅgāla twice (cp.49.m2, cp.49.m6), and the Tibetan comment has gnyis su med pa, 'nondual', in both places. Only the Tibetan verse line reads 'pitiless' (brtse ba med pas). 'Pitiless' gives the easier literal story of a robbery; 'nondual' follows the only Sanskrit witness.

I took baṅgāle as the agent, 'by Baṅgāla'. Munidatta (-vaṅgālena, instrumental) and the Tibetan line (agentive -s) both read it that way, but the -e could equally be locative, 'in Baṅgāla'. I used the glossary's 'affliction' exactly. kleśa may be plural here ('the afflictions were plundered'), which would read more naturally.

The Tibetan line, brtse ba med pas baM ga la yul khyer, 'the pitiless one carried off the land of Baṃgala', has no word for kleśa. Shastri also prints ধ্রু, the refrain cue, after this couplet, although the refrain is couplet 2. It is not translated.

Both baṅgālī and bhailī have feminine endings. I took Bhusu(ku) as the subject, with the feminine either agreeing with baṅgālī or chosen to rhyme with lelī. Munidatta reads the line as the poet addressing himself, 'O Bhusukupāda', and uses the feminine vaṅgālikā bhūtā (cp.49.m3). That allows two other readings: 'Today, Bhusu, you have become a Bengali', or '… she has become a Bengali woman', with the wife of 2b as subject.
The Tibetan line is de ring b+hu su ku pa nang 'khrug shor, 'today, Bhusukupa, inner strife broke loose (or: was lost)'. It renders baṅgālī as nang 'khrug, 'inner strife'.
The source has the short form ভূসু, Bhusu, perhaps for the metre. The English uses the glossary variant Bhusuku.

lines.en: his own [wife]{grhini} has been taken by the [Caṇḍāla]{candala}.

flags.note: Shastri prints caṇḍālī. Read as the object of lelī, 'took', that gives '(he) took a Caṇḍālī as his own wife' (the glossary hit candali). Munidatta instead cites caṇḍālena, 'by the Caṇḍāla' (cp.49.m3), and the Tibetan line has gtum pos khyer, 'carried off by the fierce one'. I chose the Caṇḍāla as agent for two reasons. Shastri's -ī can be an Old Bengali agent ending (compare cauri in song 2), and the feminine lelī then agrees with ghariṇī, 'wife', the thing taken.
'His' supplies the owner implied by ṇia, 'own', from 2a. If 2a is a self-address, this becomes 'your own wife'. The passive keeps the source order: wife first, the Caṇḍāla last.

lines.translit: ḍahi jo pañcadhāṭa ṇai dibi saṃjñā ṇaṭhā
lines.gloss: having-burned · which · pañcadhāṭa (five ghāṭas?) · river (?) · divine (?) · perception · lost
lines.en: With the [pañcadhāṭa]{pancadhata} [river]{river} burned, divine perception is lost;

flags.note: pañcadhāṭa is obscure, so it is kept in its source form. It may be pañca ghāṭa, 'five landing places' (ধ misread for ঘ). Munidatta cites it as pañcapāṭana (cp.49.m4), and the Tibetan line has rnam pa lnga po, 'the five kinds'.

I took ṇai as ṇaī, 'river', joined to pañcadhāṭa ('the pañcadhāṭa river'; if ghāṭa is right, 'the river of five landings'). It might instead go with dibi, or be a verb form. Neither Munidatta (cp.49.m4) nor the Tibetan line mentions a river.

I took dibi as divya, 'divine', with little confidence. It could be 'day' (diva), and saṃjñā might then stand for sandhyā, 'dusk' ('day and dusk are lost'). I rendered saṃjñā 'perception'; it can also mean 'consciousness', as in the idiom for fainting. I avoided 'awareness', which the glossary uses for cetanā, and 'senses', which this line's glossary entry bars and which belongs to indriya.
ḍahi means 'having burned' (Munidatta's lemma is dahia, cp.49.m4). With the relative jo, 'which', I rendered it as an absolute clause, 'With the … burned'. The song names no one who burns it.

The Tibetan line, rnam pa lnga po bsregs shing yul rnams brlag, 'the five kinds burned and the objects destroyed', has nothing for ṇai or dibi. Its 'objects' (yul) may stand for saṃjñā, or may echo the comment's senses and objects.

lines.translit: ṇa jānami cia mora kahim̐ gai paiṭhā
lines.gloss: not · I-know · mind · my · where · gone · entered
lines.en: I do not know where my [mind]{citta} has gone and entered.

flags.note: The Tibetan line adds 'jewel': rang sems rin chen gar 'gro sleb mi shes, 'I do not know where my own mind-jewel goes and arrives'. This matches Munidatta's cittaratna (cp.49.m4). The Bengali has only cia, 'mind'.

lines.translit: soṇa tarua mora kimpi ṇa thākiu
lines.gloss: gold · silver · my · anything-at-all · not · remained
lines.en: Of my [gold]{gold} and [silver]{silver} nothing at all remained;

flags.note: tarua, 'silver', follows the glossary and the Tibetan line (gser dngul, 'gold, silver'). In the comment Shastri restores the word as [ta]rua and [ta]ruya. The Tibetan comment transcribes it rU pa, which suggests its text read rua or rūpā, with no ta (cp.49.m5).

lines.en: with my own household I remained in [great bliss]{mahasukha}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line, rang gi 'khor gyis rin chen blangs nas gnas, has a jewel taken where the Bengali has great bliss. It reads either 'having taken the jewel, I stay with my own retinue' or 'my own retinue took the jewel and stays'. The Bengali has no verb for 'take'.

I took paribāre as 'with my household' and thākiu as first person, 'I remained', in line with Munidatta's 'I am immersed' (cp.49.m5). The household could instead be the subject: 'my household remained in great bliss'. The English repeats 'remained' because 4a and 4b end on the same word, thākiu.

lines.gloss: four-crore (four koṭis) · storehouse · my · taken · to-the-end
lines.en: My [storehouse]{storehouse} of [four crores]{four-crores} has been taken, all of it;

flags.note: caukoṛi: I chose 'four crores', the image of wealth, which is how the Tibetan line reads it (bye ba phrag bzhi). Munidatta reads catuṣkoṭi, the four alternatives (cp.49.m6). That is a reading of the image, so it goes in the notes.

laiā sesa is literally 'taken, (to the) end'; I rendered it 'taken, all of it'. The Tibetan has ma lus khyer, 'carried off without remainder'. The song names no taker; Munidatta supplies the nondual Vaṅgāla (cp.49.m6).
jībante and mailem̐ are oblique forms, 'in (or by) living, in dying'; I rendered them 'living or dead'. The Tibetan agrees: gson po dang ni shi la khyad par med.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Every song is headed by the rāga it is sung to, and this one is sung in Mallārī, which also heads song 30. The Bengali heading does not name the poet. His name comes from the attribution bhusukupādānām, 'of Bhusukupāda', which Shastri's text places before the song; it was removed from line 1a because it is not part of the verse.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song mal+lA ri tA la gcig pa zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the song called Mallāri tā la gcig pa, of Bhusukupāda'. The words tA la gcig pa are not in the Bengali. They probably name a tāla, a rhythmic cycle: 'of one beat', or 'in a single tāla'. They are left out of the English heading.

Read literally, the song is a run of losses on a journey by boat. Affliction is plundered, the wife is taken, and the gold, the silver and the storehouse are gone. Yet the speaker remains with his household in great bliss, and living and dying are the same to him. The refrain sums it up: today he has become a Bengali, a man of Baṅgāla, the country where the plunder happened.

Munidatta introduces the song this way: the siddha master Bhusupāda, bathed in nectar from the churning of the ocean of the perfection of wisdom, sets out the same meaning under the guise of a Bengali woman (vaṅgālikāvyājena) (cp.49.m1). The printed -tvāmṛta- is probably for tattvāmṛta, 'the nectar of reality', since the Tibetan has de kho na nyid kyi bdud rtsi. Where the Sanskrit has 'under the guise of a Bengali woman', the Tibetan has nang 'khrug gi dgongs pa'i skad kyis, 'in the intentional language of inner strife'.
In this song the poet names himself in the refrain (2a: ভূসু, Bhusu), not in the last couplet, where the bhaṇitā usually stands.

Vajra: the thunderbolt-diamond, which tantric Buddhism takes as the emblem of what cannot be destroyed. Here it is read in bāja (Sanskrit vajra), a 'vajra boat'. pāṛī is taken as Bengali pāṛi, 'a crossing'. pam̐uā may be the lotus (padma) or the Padmā, the great eastern arm of the Ganges in Bengal. The draft follows the lotus, because both old witnesses read the flower: Munidatta's paraphrase speaks of the lotus of wisdom (prajñāravinda, cp.49.m2), and the Tibetan line has a lotus grove. khāla is a canal or creek of the delta. bāhiu, 'rowed', comes from bāh-, 'to row, to ply a boat'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rgyal po'i gru ni pad+ma'i tshal nas 'bab, 'the king's boat comes down from the lotus grove'. It has 'king' (rgyal po) for bāja, perhaps reading রাজ rāja for বাজ; 'lotus grove' (pad+ma'i tshal) for the pam̐uā canal; and 'bab, 'comes down, flows down', for bāhiu, 'rowed'. pāṛī has no equivalent. The Tibetan comment uses the same verb, speaking of 'flowing down to Baṃgala' (baM ga lar 'bab pa, cp.49.m2).

Munidatta's comment on this couplet cites no words of the song as a lemma. He paraphrases: something (he does not say what) is made to enter the lake in the hollow of the lotus of wisdom by means of the true guru's feet. There it is 'rowed' (vāhita, the song's bāhiu) by the Vaṅgāla that is imperishable bliss and nondual (akṣarasukhādvayavaṅgāla), and nondifference is brought about. He supports this with a scripture: the afflictions are not separate from awakening, and no affliction arises in awakening; the notion of affliction comes from error, and error is by nature stainless (cp.49.m2).

Baṅgāla (Sanskrit Vaṅgāla) was a medieval name for a region of eastern Bengal, and the source of the name Bengal. adaa can stand for advaya, 'nondual', or adaya, 'pitiless'; both would become adaa in Old Bengali. The draft follows Munidatta, who reads the word as advaya twice (akṣarasukhādvayavaṅgālena, cp.49.m2; advayavaṅgālena, cp.49.m6). The ending -e can mark either the agent ('by') or the place ('in'); Munidatta and the Tibetan both take it as the agent. luṛiu means 'plundered' (compare Bengali luṭ, 'loot').

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line brtse ba med pas baM ga la yul khyer, 'the pitiless one carried off the land of Baṃgala'. It takes adaa as adaya, 'pitiless', and has no word for kleśa, 'affliction'. Yet the Tibetan comment has gnyis su med pa, 'nondual', in both places where Munidatta has advaya (cp.49.m2, cp.49.m6), so the Tibetan verse and the Tibetan comment disagree with each other here.

Munidatta reads Baṅgāla as nondual imperishable bliss: the boat is rowed 'by the Vaṅgāla that is imperishable bliss and nondual' (cp.49.m2). In his comment on the last couplet, this same nondual Vaṅgāla is what seizes the poet's storehouse (cp.49.m6).

Both baṅgālī, 'Bengali', and bhailī, 'became', have feminine endings. The draft reads Bhusuku as the subject. Munidatta takes the refrain as the poet speaking to himself ('O Bhusukupāda') and writes the feminine vaṅgālikā bhūtā, '(has) become a Bengali woman' (cp.49.m3). On his reading the line could be 'Today, Bhusu, you have become a Bengali', or '… she has become a Bengali woman', with the wife of 2b as subject. ভূসু, Bhusu, is a short form of the poet's name.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) gives the refrain as de ring b+hu su ku pa nang 'khrug shor / rang gi khyim mi mo ni gtum pos khyer: 'Today, Bhusukupa, inner strife broke loose; his own housewife was carried off by the fierce one.' It renders baṅgālī as nang 'khrug, 'inner strife' or 'civil war', and the Tibetan comment renders vaṅgālikā the same way (cp.49.m1, cp.49.m3). gtum po, 'the fierce one', is its word for the Caṇḍāla.

Caṇḍāla: a man of the community that caste society ranked lowest and treated as untouchable; a Caṇḍālī is a woman of that community. Shastri prints caṇḍālī. The draft follows Munidatta, who cites caṇḍālena, 'by the Caṇḍāla' (cp.49.m3), and the Tibetan line, gtum pos khyer, 'carried off by the fierce one'. Shastri's -ī can be read as an Old Bengali agent ending (compare cauri, 'by the thief', in song 2), and the feminine lelī, 'taken', agrees with ghariṇī, 'wife'. If caṇḍālī is instead the object, the line says '(he) took a Caṇḍālī as his own wife'.

Munidatta says that with the refrain the poet makes the same meaning plain, addressing himself. He reads the poet's own wife as the avadhūtī (in tantric yoga, the central channel of the subtle body) in the form of wind, and glosses 'by the Caṇḍāla' as 'led away by clear light whose nature is touch' (sparśaprakṛtiprabhāsvara) (cp.49.m3). The printed Sanskrit calls this avadhūtī unpurified (apariśuddha); the Tibetan comment instead has sems yongs su dag pa, 'the completely purified mind'.

pañcadhāṭa: a word of uncertain sense, naming something fivefold that is burned; it is kept in its source form. It may be pañca ghāṭa, 'five landing places', with ধ misread for the similar ঘ. That would give 'the river of five landings', in keeping with the boat and canal of couplet 1. Munidatta cites it as pañcapāṭana (cp.49.m4), and the Tibetan line has rnam pa lnga po, 'the five kinds'.

ḍahi means 'having burned'; Munidatta's lemma is dahia (cp.49.m4). jo, 'which', is taken to introduce the burned pañcadhāṭa. ṇai is taken as ṇaī, 'river' (Sanskrit nadī), as in bhavaṇai, 'the river of existence', in song 5. dibi is taken, doubtfully, as divya, 'divine'. saṃjñā means 'perception', and also 'consciousness'. ṇaṭhā means 'lost, destroyed' (Sanskrit naṣṭa).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rnam pa lnga po bsregs shing yul rnams brlag, 'the five kinds are burned and the objects (or lands) destroyed'. It has no river and nothing for dibi. Its 'objects' (yul) is closer to the senses and objects of the comment (cp.49.m4) than to saṃjñā.

Munidatta glosses the couplet: by that fire of great bliss, I-making, mine-making and the like, which rest on the five aggregates, are burned (his gloss of pañcapāṭana), along with the senses and their objects. Therefore, having himself given up conceptual thought, the poet does not know the mind-jewel (cittaratna). He then cites Saraha (cp.49.m4).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rang sems rin chen gar 'gro sleb mi shes, 'I do not know where my own mind-jewel goes and arrives'. It adds 'jewel' (rin chen), like Munidatta's cittaratna, 'mind-jewel' (cp.49.m4). The Bengali gai paiṭhā means 'gone (and) entered' (Sanskrit gata, praviṣṭa).

tarua is taken as 'silver', as in the Tibetan line, gser dngul, 'gold and silver'. In the comment Shastri restores the word as [ta]rua and [ta]ruya. The Tibetan comment transcribes it rU pa (cp.49.m5), which suggests a text reading rua or rūpā, Bengali for 'silver', with no ta.

Munidatta glosses 'gold' as grasping at emptiness and 'silver' as grasping at being. When both concepts are examined in their true nature, nothing at all remains. He explains 'with my own household' (nijaparivāreṇa) with a near-homophone, nirvikalpaparihāreṇa, 'by giving up conceptual thought', and goes on: 'I am immersed in the jewel of great bliss' (cp.49.m5). The Tibetan comment takes the phrase the same way (nges par rnam par rtog pa spangs pas).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rang gi 'khor gyis rin chen blangs nas gnas: 'having taken the jewel, I stay with my own retinue', or 'my own retinue took the jewel and stays'. It has 'jewel' and 'taken' where the Bengali has 'great bliss'. Compare Munidatta's 'jewel of great bliss' (mahāsukharatna, cp.49.m5).
paribāra: household or family; also a retinue. thākiu, 'remained', is the same word that ends 4a, where nothing remains, so the English repeats 'remained'.

caukoṛi means 'four koṭis'. A koṭi, or crore, is ten million, so this is the worth of the storehouse, as the Tibetan line reads it (bye ba phrag bzhi, 'four ten-millions'). Koṭi also means 'point' or 'alternative', and Munidatta takes the word as catuṣkoṭi, the four alternatives of Madhyamaka reasoning (cp.49.m6). bhaṇḍāra means 'storehouse, treasury' and laiā 'taken'. sesa (Sanskrit śeṣa, 'end') here means 'entirely', like the Tibetan ma lus, 'without remainder'.

Munidatta glosses the couplet: the poet's storehouse of examination by the four alternatives has been seized by that nondual Vaṅgāla, so in him there is no conceptual thought of living, dying, meditation and the like. He cites the Hevajra (cp.49.m6). The Tibetan comment calls the one who carries it off nang 'khrug pa, 'the one of inner strife'. Where the Sanskrit says the couplet speaks of absolute nonexistence (atyantābhāva), the Tibetan has thorough meditation (shin tu bsgoms pa), as if it read atyantabhāvanā.

termsOmitted.reason: Shastri's caṇḍālī is read as the agent, 'by the Caṇḍāla', following Munidatta's caṇḍālena (cp.49.m3) and the Tibetan gtum pos khyer, so the line is marked {candala}. If the reviewer keeps Shastri's object reading ('took a Caṇḍālī as his own wife'), mark [Caṇḍālī]{candali} instead.
This hit is only in the Tibetan line (pad+ma'i tshal, 'lotus grove'). The Bengali has a canal (khālem̐), marked {canal}; the Tibetan reading is reported in a witness note.
This is a Tibetan-side hit only, and a false one: yul here is part of baM ga la yul, 'the land of Baṃgala', not 'sense objects'.
This hit is only in the Tibetan line (yul rnams brlag, 'the objects destroyed'). The Bengali has no word for sense objects, and the term's own reading is reported in the witness note.
This hit is only in the Tibetan line (rang sems rin chen, 'my own mind-jewel'). The Bengali has only cia, 'mind'. Reported in a witness note.
This hit is only in the Tibetan line (rin chen blangs, 'took the jewel'). The Bengali has mahāsuhe, 'in great bliss'. Reported in a witness note.
This is a Tibetan-side hit only, and a false one: lus is part of ma lus, 'without remainder', not 'body'.

questions: 1b adaa: I chose advaya, 'nondual', following Munidatta (cp.49.m2, cp.49.m6) and the Tibetan comment. The Tibetan verse line reads adaya, 'pitiless' (brtse ba med pas), which gives an easier literal story of a robbery ('affliction was plundered by pitiless Baṅgāla'). Which do you want in the line?

2b caṇḍālī: I read it as the agent, 'his own wife has been taken by the Caṇḍāla' ({candala}), with Munidatta's caṇḍālena and the Tibetan gtum pos khyer. Do you prefer Shastri's text as it stands, '(he) took a Caṇḍālī as his own wife' ({candali})? The choice changes the story: in one he loses his wife to an outcaste man, in the other he marries an outcaste woman.

1a pam̐uā: I chose 'lotus canal', as both old witnesses read it. Would you rather have 'the Padmā canal' (the river), which fits Baṅgāla in 1b? That would need a place entry such as pl-padma, which I have not proposed.
1a bāja: is 'vajra boat' acceptable? The Tibetan line's 'king's boat' (rgyal po'i gru) looks like a reading of রাজ for বাজ.

3a is the least secure line: pañcadhāṭa, ṇai ('river'?) and dibi ('divine'?) are all doubtful. For saṃjñā I used 'perception', avoiding 'awareness' (the glossary's cetanā) and 'senses' (barred in this line, and the glossary's indriya). Should saṃjñā get its own glossary entry?

2a: is the third person ('Today Bhusuku has become a Bengali') right, or would you follow Munidatta's self-address ('Today, Bhusu, you have become a Bengali'; cp.49.m3)? Both baṅgālī and bhailī are feminine.
2a: the source has the short form Bhusu (ভূসু). I used the glossary variant 'Bhusuku'. Should 'Bhusu' be added as a variant so the refrain can keep the poet's own short form?
1b: I used the glossary form 'affliction' exactly, as a mass noun. May the line use the plural, 'the afflictions were plundered', which reads more naturally?
5a: I kept the image, 'four crores', and left Munidatta's four alternatives to the notes. Please confirm.

Heading: the Tibetan adds tA la gcig pa, probably a tāla, 'one beat'. I recorded it only in a witness note. The glossary's existing 'tala' is a different word (ṭāla, song 33). Should a musical tāla be glossed if more Tibetan headings carry it?
